one_liner: Rive's C++ runtime and GPU vector renderer (Metal, Vulkan, D3D, GL); vendor claims 66x Skia on animated tiles.
what_it_does: rive-runtime loads .riv files, advances artboards, animations and state machines, and draws through an abstract rive::Renderer interface. The built-in GPU renderer (RiveRenderer over a RenderContext with RenderContextImpl backends for Metal, Vulkan, D3D11, D3D12, OpenGL/WebGL and WebGPU) also accepts arbitrary paths and paints, so it can be used as a general 2D path renderer, but its API is Rive's own (RenderPath, RenderPaint, beginFrame/flush), not Skia's SkCanvas. The repo also ships a Skia adapter (skia/) and a CoreGraphics renderer (cg_renderer/) that implement the same Renderer interface.
how_it_is_fast: Paths are not stenciled or CPU-rasterized: curves are tessellated on the GPU (Wang's formula picks segment counts; TessVertexSpan rows are rendered into a tessellation texture) and drawn as 'midpoint fan' triangle patches with analytic anti-aliased coverage, or, for large filled paths, through a cached interior triangulation (a Skia-derived GrInnerFanTriangulator) gated by a TriangulationController. Coverage and per-path 16-bit IDs live in pixel local storage, so many paths batch into one pass without clearing a coverage buffer; overlapping fragments are synchronized per platform by an InterlockMode (rasterOrdering via Metal raster order groups or GL framebuffer fetch / EXT/ANGLE PLS, atomics, clockwise, clockwiseAtomic, or an MSAA depthStencil fallback). A SIMD IntersectionBoard (255x255 tiles, int16x8 lanes) groups non-overlapping draws so they can share a batch, and GPU buffers are ring-allocated (3 frames) so CPU preparation overlaps GPU rendering.
when_to_use: Shipping Rive (.riv) animations in a C++ app, game engine or embedded UI: this is the reference renderer behind Rive's Apple, Android, Flutter, Unity, Unreal and web runtimes.
Many animated, path-heavy vector layers per frame on Apple GPUs (iOS and Apple Silicon Macs), where Metal raster order groups give the fully featured rasterOrdering mode.

GPU vector rendering on Android GL ES devices exposing EXT_shader_pixel_local_storage or framebuffer fetch, or on Vulkan/D3D12 desktops, when CPU rasterization (Blend2D, Skia CPU) is the frame-time bottleneck.
You already render through Rive's abstract Renderer and want to swap a Skia or CoreGraphics backend for the native GPU one without changing scene code.
when_not_to_use: You need a drop-in SkCanvas replacement, PDF/SVG output, text shaping APIs outside Rive's text system, or CPU-only/headless rendering: there is no CPU rasterizer backend (RenderContextNULL only counts work for benchmarks).

Hardware without PLS-class features: WebGL and many GL drivers fall back to atomics or the MSAA depthStencil mode, and open issue #83 (Feb 2026, unanswered) asks how to get PLS on WebGL at all; the 66x claim came from an iPhone, the best case.

Build-system constraints: it builds with premake via build/build_rive.sh, which clones a pinned premake and fetches Vulkan-Headers, VulkanMemoryAllocator, DirectX-Headers, harfbuzz (Rive fork) and python ply from GitHub at configure time, then compiles shaders with a make + Python minifier step; there is no CMake package and issue #69 asks for prebuilt libraries.

Mature D3D11 or Linux GL deployments without testing: open issues include #99 (D3D11 access violation in makeImageTexture), #57 (invalid DX resource flags fail renderer init) and #92 (OpenGL context fails on Linux).
Many identical sprites: issue #81 (open) notes each Rive instance is its own draw, with no GPU instancing across artboards.

integration.form: static lib (librive.a plus librive_pls_renderer.a, built with premake)
integration.dependencies: Platform GPU SDK (Metal/Xcode, Vulkan SDK, Windows SDK for D3D, GL/WebGL); configure-time GitHub downloads of Vulkan-Headers, VulkanMemoryAllocator, DirectX-Headers, python ply (shader minifier) and Rive's forks or pins of harfbuzz (rive-app/harfbuzz rive_13.1.1), SheenBidi, yoga and miniaudio for text, layout and audio; optional rive decoders for images
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; clang (Xcode CLI tools on macOS, distro clang on Linux), clang-cl or MSVC with Visual Studio 2022 on Windows; bash, git and Python 3 for the build
integration.platforms: iOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS (Metal), Android (GL ES, Vulkan), Windows (D3D11, D3D12, GL, Vulkan), Linux (GL, Vulkan), WebAssembly (WebGL2, WebGPU)
integration.thread_safety: A RenderContext is driven from one render thread per frame; render_context.hpp comments describe a recording session (DeferredSession) on a producer thread while the render thread is inside a frame, and an atomic added to fix a data race there. Broader guarantees not documented.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — scene code written against rive::Renderer can swap the Skia backend (skia/) for RiveRenderer, but there is no SkCanvas-compatible API for general Skia users

gotchas: Feature set depends on InterlockMode: atomics mode masks out nested clipping and modulated images, and clockwise/clockwiseAtomic modes override every path's fill rule (no even-odd), per ShaderFeaturesMaskFor in gpu.hpp.

Per-device quirks are handled in code: pre-Apple-Silicon iOS PowerVR GPUs drop the low 3 bits of path IDs for fp16 precision, the iOS simulator has no framebuffer reads and falls back to atomics, and ANGLE devices run a runtime test before trusting KHR_blend_equation_advanced.
The build fetches pinned third-party repos from GitHub and runs a shader make step during premake configuration, so offline or hermetic builds need those mirrored.
tests/bench micro-benchmarks run against RenderContextNULL (CPU-side draw preparation only) and print the minimum time over a 5 s loop; they measure no GPU time and no Skia baseline.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over ThorVG or TGFX when your content is Rive animation or you want a renderer whose hot path is GPU PLS coverage rather than a CPU raster backend; pick vkvg or vger only for simpler Vulkan/Metal UI drawing, and Blend2D when you need fast, portable CPU rendering with an independent benchmark behind it.
verified_claims_summary: The only speed number is Rive's own LinkedIn post (dated 2023-05-05, derived from its activity ID, so about ten months before the renderer was open-sourced): on an 'iPhone 12 Max', Skia drew 9 animated Rive tiles in about 100 ms while the Rive Renderer drew 100 tiles in about 16 ms (and 36 tiles in about 5 ms), stated as 66x or 6000 vs 90 tiles/sec. The Skia backend and settings, the measured code version and the harness are not published (the post is snippet-only here), and no third-party measurement was found.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-03, about 3,300 commits) and MIT-licensed, so copyable, but it is a large engine with its own build system rather than a vendorable library, and the speed claim is first-party marketing.
sources_read: WebSearch: Rive Renderer vs Skia Impeller benchmark frame time measured (snippet of https://www.linkedin.com/posts/guidorosso_the-rive-renderer-is-66x-faster-here-activity-7060336385030819841-QkSZ)
